newsitem.title: FRANCE: CGT union attacks French civil service pay offer.
newsitem.headline: CGT union attacks French civil service pay offer.

text.p: The French government, confronted with the prospect of a strike, offered civil servants a 2.8-percent pay rise for 1997-98 on Tuesday but no "catch up" for a 1996 pay freeze, the Communist-led CGT trade union said.

The CGT, the first to meet Civil Service Minister Dominique Perben on Tuesday, attacked the offer and said in a statement "what is important in the face of this kind of attitude is that employees make themselves heard loud and clear."
Unions had warned in advance that they would fight any offer that failed to make at least a gesture to compensate for a pay freeze in 1996 and that they were considering a March strike.

Perben was meeting the unions one-by-one to reveal the pay offer which concerns millions of civil servants in the central administration, teachers, health sector staff and employees of local public authorities.
The unions are due to meet at 1800 GMT to decide on their response.
The 1996 civil service pay freeze was one of several union gripes behind crippling public sector strikes in late 1995.
The CGT said Perben made it clear there was "no question" of dealing with the 1996 pay freeze in the latest pay round.
"Is this the kind of framework in which the minister asks about the possibility of opening 'negotiations'?" the militant CGT said in its statement.
"Negotiate what? A fall in purchasing power? New widespread losses due to the spreading-out (of the pay rise) envisaged?"

"The minister's announcement is a non-event. It was expected and is part of a policy which attacks purchasing power, public employment and the public service in the forced march of the convergence criteria (for European monetary union)," it said.
The ministry would not comment but Perben was expected to hold a news conference after meeting all unions at 1700 GMT.

Pierre Avignon, leader of the moderate white-collar CGC union said last Wednesday that unions were expecting an offer that would fall short of their demands and would consider a strike in response if this turned out to be the case.
"We have decided to meet that evening (today, Tuesday) and, possibly announce a strike call," Avignon, secretary general of the CGC's civil service branch, told Reuters at the time.
He said March, after school holidays in February, would be a "logical" time for any action.
Civil servants staged a one-day strike on October 17 over pay and government plans to cut their number by nearly 6,000 this year under the 1997 budget.

The strike was followed by about a third of civil servants, according to the civil service ministry, and unions held off on follow-up action when Prime Minister Alain Juppe signalled at the time that pay talks could be reopened.
